Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Darryl, a 42-year-old electrician of Pacific Islander background, had been working long days for years and was used to finishing jobs after dark, when tools were packed away and the streets were quieter. The assault happened on one such evening, at roughly the same time of day he now found hardest to tolerate. He had been leaving a site after a routine call-out when the ordinary sounds around him changed shape in his mind: a door opening somewhere nearby, then slamming sharply, and then the sudden sense that something was wrong. What followed was not recalled by Darryl as a smooth sequence but as a few hard-edged pictures that seemed to sit apart from one another. He described seeing the scene in brief snapshots, each moment like a separate photograph: the place, the threat, his own body in it. Even now, when he tries to think about it, the account never fills in properly. Large parts feel missing, as though he can only reach fragments and the rest has been cut away. What he does remember arrives with an overwhelming sense of guilt. He returns to those moments and feels intensely responsible, as if the assault says something true about the sort of person he is. He was certain, in the aftermath, that somebody else would not have ended up in that situation, and that thought has stayed with him.

In the weeks that followed, Darryl began to notice that the same time of day would bring on a particular shift in how he felt. As evening approached, he would find himself beginning to detach, as if the world had moved a little farther away and he were becoming unreal in it. He did not experience this as an abstract fear but as a bodily, unsettling drift that made him pause and check himself. The change was especially sharp when a door banged somewhere in the house, or when a door at work or in a shop opened too suddenly; the sound would jolt him back into the assault before he could settle. He also became wary of unexpected movement nearby. If someone moved quickly beside him, even in an ordinary setting, his body reacted before he had time to think, as though danger were present again. He found the same thing happening when someone touched him without warning. A hand on his arm, a tap on the shoulder, even a casual brush in passing could bring an immediate alarmed reaction that embarrassed him afterward, though at the moment it felt automatic and unavoidable.

Darryl’s days gradually narrowed around what felt manageable. He began spending long hours on his phone, games, and the internet, letting himself disappear into screens for stretches that were much longer than he intended. At night, and sometimes during breaks, he would keep scrolling or gaming simply so he would not have to think. He also started drinking more than he had before and used medication or drugs at times to blunt what was coming up in his mind. He avoided television programmes, films, and anything he might read that reminded him of similar events, not because he wanted to be uninformed but because he could not bear the images they might bring into his head. In the months after the assault, this pattern affected both his relationship and his work. His partner noticed how often he was off on his phone and how present he was not during conversations, while at work he became more guarded in unfamiliar places. He avoided going to new sites or places he could not assess in advance, feeling he could not judge where the danger might be. That meant he sometimes turned down opportunities or relied on the most familiar routes and settings, limiting the way he moved through both job and daily life.

By the time Darryl came to treatment, he was living with the constant sense that he had no future and that the attack had revealed something final about him. He was not speaking as someone looking back on one bad event but as someone who felt that the event had narrowed his life to a set of predictable alarms, gaps in memory, and a future that had already been taken away. What brought him in was the accumulation of those fears: the startle at doors and movement, the unease when touched, the pull to disappear into screens or drink, and the growing sense that his world was shrinking around what he could no longer face. He came hoping, if possible, to feel less on edge and less trapped by the memory fragments that still arrived at the same hour each day, but he was most afraid that nothing would change and that the assault had already decided who he was and what would happen next.
